title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: 28 officials targeted in recalls over data center votes—what it means for your town.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy—the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Sunday morning, August 23, and we're diving into the growing pushback against these massive projects—starting with a new look at how local officials are paying a political price.
Yeah, this feels like it's hitting a new level.
Our big story today comes from a Bridge Michigan analysis out this week showing at least 28 officials across eight communities facing recall efforts tied directly to their data center votes.
Only one of those recalls has made it onto the November ballot so far?
That's right. The piece tracks how these fights are playing out in townships and cities from the Upper Peninsula down through western and southeast Michigan.
So why are residents turning to recalls instead of just voting no on the projects themselves?

A lot of it comes down to timing and process. Proposals pop up, officials hold hearings or votes on rezoning and permits, and neighbors feel blindsided by the scale—noise, traffic, water use, power demand.
We've seen that pattern in a bunch of places just this week.
Exactly. Yesterday in one township they rejected a server farm on Kluver Road after residents raised those exact concerns. The rural character stays intact for now.
And over in South Haven, neighbors are fighting a rezoning that could open the door to a data center on the Baseline property.
Same worries—noise, traffic, strain on services. These decisions are setting precedents for nearby communities.
What about the bigger picture on power and water? How much does one of these things actually pull?

We're talking facilities that can demand hundreds of megawatts—sometimes scaling toward a gigawatt. That kind of load can push up electric rates for everyone on the grid if utilities have to build new generation or transmission.
And water for cooling?
Millions of gallons a day in some cases. Townships are hearing from residents worried about wells running low or higher utility bills to cover infrastructure upgrades.
Farmland is another big one, right?

Yes—prime agricultural land getting converted, or at least the threat of it. In places like St. Joseph County they're debating a two-year moratorium to study road, water, and electricity impacts before more proposals move forward.
That sounds like a direct response to the pressure.
It is. And in Palmyra Township in Lenawee County, residents packed a session Friday voicing fears about spiking electric bills and constant noise from the proposed sites.
Anyone within 50 miles could feel the utility cost ripple if these go through without tighter rules.
Then there's the Forsyth Township meeting yesterday in the U.P.—hundreds showed up to grill officials on power rates, water supplies, and even rumors of military ties near the Marquette County sites.
First real look at the scale for a lot of those residents.
Meanwhile, a developer is suing Gibraltar to overturn a year-long moratorium, claiming it illegally blocked their project. Wayne County folks could see delayed tax revenue and jobs if the suit wins.
That tests how far local governments can actually go to hit pause on these.
On the developer side, the firm behind the Mason project in Ingham County was finally named on Friday. Gives residents a clearer target for questions on water, noise, and grid impact.
And Hyperscale Data sold $43 million in Bitcoin Friday to fund their Michigan push—cut debt by $30 million too.
Crypto volatility directly feeding local infrastructure plans. Michigan residents will see it in added power demand and potential tax deals.
So how does all this feed into the recall numbers?

The Bridge analysis shows the recalls are concentrated in communities where officials approved or advanced projects despite vocal opposition. Residents feel their voices weren't heard at the hearing stage.
Is this new, or has it been building?
It's accelerating. Data center proposals have multiplied across western Michigan townships in the last year or so, and the local fights are now hitting the political accountability layer.
What happens next with these recalls?
Most are still in the signature-gathering phase. Only one has qualified for November so far. Success depends on whether organizers can hit the required thresholds before deadlines.
And if they do qualify, does that change how other townships handle future proposals?
It could. Officials watching these races might lean toward more pauses or stricter conditions to avoid becoming targets themselves.
We've also got Saline residents voicing fears Friday about power costs and lost tax revenue if projects win big breaks.
Dozens at a coffee hour in Washtenaw County—another sign the issue is becoming a flashpoint.
So the recalls aren't happening in a vacuum. They're part of this broader wave of community pushback.
Right. The analysis puts a number on it—28 officials across eight communities—but the underlying driver is the same everywhere: scale of the projects versus local resources.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
Signature drives, more public hearings, and whether any of these recalls actually force a special election or change a board's makeup.
And how developers respond—more lawsuits like the one in Gibraltar, or more outreach?
Both are possible. The Gibraltar case could set a legal precedent on moratoriums.
Meanwhile the power and water questions keep coming up in every township.
Exactly. One gigawatt-scale facility can reshape the local grid and aquifer conversation for years.
So the recalls are a symptom of deeper tensions over who decides and who pays.
That's the heart of it. Residents want more say before the concrete is poured.
All right, let's move to some quick hits from the last couple days.
Yesterday a township rejected the Kluver Road server farm permit after noise, traffic, and water concerns from nearby residents.
Keeps that rural area free of large-scale projects for now.
Also yesterday, South Haven neighbors ramped up opposition to rezoning the Baseline property for the same reasons.
A decision there could influence similar fights in surrounding townships.
In the U.P., hundreds turned out in Forsyth Township to question power rates, water, and rumored military connections.
First direct public look at the Marquette County proposals.
On Friday the Mason project developer was finally identified—Ingham County residents now have a name to direct questions to.
Clarity on who’s behind the power and tax impacts.
St. Joseph County is weighing a two-year freeze while they study roads, water, and electricity.
Residents there are worried about higher bills and lost farmland.
Saline held a Friday coffee hour where dozens pressed leaders on electric bills, water, and tax breaks.
Flashpoint status confirmed in Washtenaw County.
Hyperscale Data offloaded 685 Bitcoin for $43 million on Friday specifically to fund their Michigan buildout.
Crypto cash flowing into local power and water demands.
And Palmyra Township residents pushed back Friday over power spikes and noise from proposed sites.
Lenawee County joins the list of communities voicing the same concerns.
Now for what's on deck—upcoming meetings listeners can attend.
Tomorrow, August 24, the Planning Commission is reviewing a new site plan application for the Verrus data center project.
Check your local notices for time and location if you want to weigh in.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Recall Pressure Builds as Michigan Data Center Fights Spread
